speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think this motion should be adopted, because it would be a departure from a well established rule that has been in force in England for many years and in this country since at least the days when Sir John Thompson was Minister of Justice. All the successors of Sir John Thompson-Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, Sir Allen Aylesworth, Right Hon. Charles Doherty, and Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier speaking as leader of the Opposition, when they had occasion to express their views on the subject, were of the opinion that such documents should be treated as confidential and that it would not be proper or advisable to make them public. The practice in England is well defined by Todd, and I think that one citation from that authority will be enough to cover all that has been said on the question. I quote from Todd's Parliamentary Government in England, page 557:
No interference by either House of parliament with the exercise of this prerogative is justifiable, except under extraordinary circumstances. It was said by Macaulay, that he would rather entrust it to the hands of the very worst ministry that ever held office than allow it to be exercised under the direction of the very best House of Commons; and by Sir Robert Peel, that he would leave this prerogative in the hands of the executive considering that it was the right and duty of the House to interfere only if there be a suspicion that justice is perverted for corrupt purposes.
In this special case, Mr. Speaker, I have read the record. I do not see anything extraordinary in it, and I do not see why we should make an exception in this case. Taking into account such a rule and such a practice I would ask my hon. friend not to press his motion.

In view of the authorities cited by the hon. Minister of Justice I have no desire to press the motion.
Motion withdrawn.

Hon. W. S. FIELDING moved the second reading of Bill No. 23 respecting a certain Convention * of Commerce between His Majesty and the French Republic.

A few days ago, in discussing this treaty, I pointed out to the House the great disadvantage that
certain of the farmers in the part of Ontario I come from would labour under if it went into effect in its present form. I have particular reference to the farmers in my district who are interested in the growing of grapes and in the manufacture of wine. It seems to me that a grave injustice has been done to these people. I cannot comprehend how any government would undertake to put the residents of a foreign country in an absolutely better position than their own people. In the present case the people in my district are paying to the revenue of the country a tax of 30 cents a gallon on wine, and under this treaty the French article is to be allowed to come in at a tax of only 15 cents a gallon. In other woids, the producer in a foreign country is at a direct advantage in this country's market of 15 cents a gallon. I do not want to stress the matter but the thing is self-evidently unjust and I believe it must be taken care of.
I also referred briefly to a matter of importance to our particular section, and that was the silk industry. I do not want to unduly emphasize this point, but I want to look into some of the points of interest in connection with the treaty and ask this House to judge whether it is of any advantage to Canada.
The first part of the treaty I wish to take up is what is known as section A, which gives a list of goods of Canadian production that are allowed to enter France under their minimum tariff. I might say incidentally that while this schedule A is the minimum tariff of France, last year we had almost the whole of it as the minimum tariff of France. I mean, that all the goods that we wanted to ship last year of that class and variety entered France practically under the minimum tariff. Before I go into the details I want to point out that the imports to Canada from France for the year ending 31st March, 1922, amounted to 813,500,000, whereas the exports from Canada to France for the same period amounted to $8,000,000. I wish to explain to the House that, in making my calculations, I have not taken into account the colonies of France, for the reason that there were so many small items spread over half a dozen countries that it made the work too heavy, and I did not have any clerk from the department to help me. Just for comparison's sake, I wish to state that during the same period we exported to Holland $9,500,000. I am taking four or five countries with exports about similar so that hon. members can see at a glance what the significance is. During that period we exported $9,500,000 to Holland and we imported from Holland $4,000,000. I am only giving the round figures. Then we exported to Belgium $12,400,000 and

we imported from Belgium $3,800,000. We exported to Italy $15,000,000 and imported $1,300,000. We exported to Japan $14,800,000 and imported from Japan $8,000,000. To these four countries we exported $52,000,000, and imported from them $17,000,000, leaving a balance in our favour for these four countries of $34,000,000, whereas the balance against us in France was $5,000,000.
I think possibly I will have to apologize to the House for taking up considerable time in going through these items, but inasmuch as the two ministers spent five months on the job, I think possibly the' House can hear somebody else for an hour. The first item in schedule A is horses. We had the minimum tariff of France last year for horses, and there has been no change this year from the tariff of last year. We exported last year horses to the value of $1,000,000, but we did not send a dollar's worth to France. I ask the minister if he did not send any horses to France last year, and there has not been any change to our advantage, what chance will there be next year? The price of horses was low last year and we might have had an export.

I now wish to refer for a moment, but only in a general' way, to some of the articles that France is allowed to sell Canada under this treaty. I would ask the Minister of Finance why shrubs, ' grape vines, gooseberry bushes, and trees of all kinds of which we have good growers in this country and of which we export considerable quantities are allowed to enter Canada at two cents apiece whereas similar provision has not been made for Canadian trees and shrubs on the part of France. It seems to me that there should be extended to us the same privileges that the other party to the treaty enjoys, otherwise this arrangement cannot be considered in any sense as a treaty. The same thing applies to other articles. The Minister of Finance admits French automobiles to Canada at a duty of 25 per cent, whereas the Canadian automobile going into France 
is subject to a duty of 45 per cent. The French piano is admitted to Canada at 25 per cent, but when the Canadian piano goes into France it must pay 35 per cent duty.
In view of this discrimination, this arrangement does not look to be very much of a treaty. Now take buggies. The rate of duty on a Canadian buggy entering France is 35 per cent; the duty on the French buggy entering Canada is only 25 per cent. The samq thing is true of buckles, needles and pins, braces and suspenders. The duty is lower on the French articles entering Canada than it is on the Canadian articles entering France. Why is it that buttons that are manufactured in this country cannot enter France on the same terms as French buttons ' are admitted to Canada? There is no use in going over the entire list of articles that enter Canada from France. All these goods that I have enumerated enter Canada under special terms. Now this is going to have a prejudicial effect on the revenues of Canada and we shall not enjoy any countervailing advantage, because, as I have shown, under this treaty no greater volume of Canadian goods will be admitted to France than went to that country last year What advantage are we going to get in return for this loss of revenue? I can quite understand that there might be some advantage to us if the effect of this treaty would be to increase the volume of our exports to France, but such will not be the case.
Having occupied so much time in dealing with this matter I feel that I owe an apology to the House. However, as two members of the government went to Europe and spent some months in the negotiation of this treaty, perhaps not very much complaint can be made if a few hon. members should occupy an hour or two in criticizing the provisions of that agreement.

speechtext:
I shall not at this late hour enter into any lengthy reply to my hon friend. I will deal only with one or. two points and then ask that six o'clock be called, 'because if I got into a detailed discussion of the question at this period of the afternoon it might be inconvenient.
I have difficulty in quite understanding th& basis of my hon. friends criticism. If I may sum it up-and I hope I sum it up correctlj -what he means to argue is this:	Our trade
with France is so inconsiderable that it is not worth our while to have a treaty with that country. I think that is a fair summary of my hon. friend's statement. If I have correctly defined his position in that regard all I have to say is that holding that view he will

French Treaty
be wise if lie records his vote when the time comes against the adoption of this treaty; there is no other course open to him. But in doing so my hon. friend will cast some little reflection upon some distinguished statesmen who have figured in this matter in the days gone by. Hitherto it has been assumed in Canada by every government, by every party, that it was desirable to have a treaty with France. It was for that reason that, long ago, Sir Charles Tupper was sent over to negotiate a treaty. It was for that reason that other members of the Conservative party were sent to negotiate a treaty with France. It was for that reason that the late government, not many months ago, made a treaty with France, a treaty to which some of the hon. gentleman's criticism applies today. It ivas for that reason my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) declared in this House that it was desirable we should have a treaty with France. It was for that reason that they put in their last trade agreement the announcement that such treaty was only of a temporary character, and that there were to be negotiations for a larger and more comprehensive convention. So when my hon. friend has established to his own satisfaction that owing to the inconsiderable volume of our trade with France we should have no treaty at all, then I say, he has done it at the expense of the reputation of the distinguished statesmen of the Conservative party in years gone by.
My hon. friend has talked about another question. He repeatedly said that in this treaty we are giving a certain rate of duty to French goods coming into Canada, while France will not give us the same rate of duty. "Why," he says, "Is that fair? Is it fair that France should send an article into Canada at a rate of 20 per cent while our goods from Canada are charged 35 per cent?" Triumphantly my hon. friend asked that question and I suppose he thinks he has got the answer to it. Well, Canada has her own fiscal policy. She has a moderate tariff policy with an inclination downward. France, on the other hand, has a high protective policy with an inclination upward. Does my hon. friend think he can change the whole fiscal policy of France at a breath? We have the greatest respect for his knowledge, and even for his skill, as a business man. But does he think that if he had gone over to Paris, like the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) and myself, he could have changed the whole fiscal policy of France, and that he could have got France to say, "We made a mistake. We are a protective country and, owing to the
war, and other reasons, we had to increase our tariff on account of the conditions which resulted, but we were wrong and we are quite prepared to revise our whole tariff policy." Does iny hon. friend think he could have accomplished that in Paris? If he does not think so then his criticism with regard to the inequality of the duties falls to the ground. Canada is a low tariff country. My hon. friend opposite may not think so; but we think we have a moderate tariff policy as against the high tariff policy of France, and if we are to trade with France in any degree we have to accept that condition; we have to accept the conditions she lays down and that is one of the vital things that my hon. friend has ignored.
The one great object, and the greatest object we had in negotiating the treaty, was this; we knew very well that we could not get low rates in France, but there was the danger that our great competitor and rival, the neighbouring republic, would get better rates, and the main policy we had in view in the negotiation was to be in a position to declare that, though the rates were high, we got the best rates that were going, the best rates granted to our competitor, the United States. That was the main feature of our tariff policy in the treaty negotiation and that has been carried out to the uttermost. I move that the debate be now adjourned.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
